text: The speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792 kilometers per second, a physical constant used to define the meter since 1983.
The Chandrasekhar limit, approximately 1.4 solar masses, defines the maximum mass at which a white dwarf star can remain stable against gravitational collapse.
Current cosmological measurements place the age of the universe at approximately 13.8 billion years, based on observations of the cosmic microwave background.
The Hubble constant, which describes the rate of cosmic expansion, is measured at approximately 70 kilometers per second per megaparsec.
Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, has an estimated mass of 4.3 million solar masses and lies about 26,000 light-years from Earth.
Voyager 1 was launched in September 1977 and crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, making it the most distant human-made object.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021 and operates near the Sun-Earth L2 point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
The Sun contains about 99.86 percent of the total mass in the solar system and has a radius of approximately 696,000 kilometers.
Earth completes one orbit around the Sun in 365.25 days at an average distance of 149.6 million kilometers, defined as one astronomical unit.
Proxima Centauri, the nearest known star to the Sun, lies approximately 4.24 light-years away in the Alpha Centauri system.
The Milky Way galaxy spans roughly 100,000 light-years in diameter and contains an estimated 200 billion stars.
Neutron star material is so dense that a single teaspoon would have a mass of roughly 10 million tons.
The cosmic microwave background radiation has a temperature of approximately 2.725 kelvin and was first detected in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson.
Albert Einstein published his general theory of relativity in 1915, describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995, was the first exoplanet found orbiting a Sun-like star.
The International Space Station orbits Earth at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing one full orbit approximately every 90 minutes.
Halley's Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years and was last visible from Earth in 1986.
NASA's Kepler space telescope, active from 2009 to 2018, confirmed the discovery of over 2,600 exoplanets.
One light-year, the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year, is equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both discovered by astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system, with a mass about 318 times that of Earth.
In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope produced the first direct image of a black hole, M87*, estimated to have a mass of 6.5 billion solar masses.
The pulsar PSR J1748-2446ad is the fastest-spinning neutron star known, rotating approximately 716 times per second.
The observable universe has a diameter of about 93 billion light-years, larger than its age in light-years due to the expansion of space.
The escape velocity needed to leave Earth's gravitational field from the surface is approximately 11.2 kilometers per second.
